content.caveat: Chirality is relative to a declared transformation group and an orientation-preserving subgroup; it is not an intrinsic word without that context.
content.exact: For x in X, define the mirror image r·x. The object x is chiral relative to (G,H) iff r·x is not in the H-orbit H·x. Because H has index 2, the property is independent of which r in G\H is chosen.
content.example: Left and right hands are the usual physical analogy: a mirror swaps handedness, while rotations alone do not.
content.plain: A chiral object has a handedness: mirroring changes it in a way that allowed orientation-preserving motions cannot undo.

assumptions.text: (X,d) is a metric space.
T:X→X is a map.

content.caveat: Sensitivity alone is not a universal definition of chaos.
content.exact: T has sensitive dependence on initial conditions iff there exists δ>0 such that for every x in X and every ε>0 there exist y in X and n>=0 with d(x,y)<ε and d(T^n(x),T^n(y))>δ.
content.example: In chaotic systems, small initial discrepancies may become macroscopically separated under iteration.
content.plain: Sensitivity formalizes one kind of error amplification: no matter how closely two starting states are chosen, some nearby state can eventually move a definite distance away.

assumptions.text: An index set I and codomain X are specified.

content.exact: A sequence in X indexed by I is a function a:I→X. When I=N, the value at n is written a_n.
content.example: The sequence 1,2,4,8,... can be represented by a_n=2^n for n=0,1,2,...
content.plain: A sequence is not merely a written list; mathematically it is a function whose input is an index.

assumptions.text: An observation model and a target inference or objective are specified.

content.caveat: The same variation can be signal for one task and noise for another; the distinction is not intrinsic to raw data alone.
content.exact: A common additive model is Y=S+N, where S is the target component and N a noise component. The decomposition is meaningful only relative to assumptions about S,N and the task.
content.example: In repeated measurements, independent zero-mean measurement error may be modeled as noise around a common signal.
content.plain: Signal is the part treated as informative for a task; noise is the part treated as nuisance, uncertainty, or unresolved variation.

assumptions.text: A notion of perturbation, a reference behavior, and a time evolution are specified.

content.caveat: There are many inequivalent notions of stability: Lyapunov, asymptotic, structural, orbital, input-output, stochastic, and others.
content.exact: For a fixed point x* of a map F on a metric space, Lyapunov stability means: for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that d(x0,x*)<δ implies d(F^n(x0),x*)<ε for all n≥0.
content.example: For F(x)=x/2 on R, x*=0 is asymptotically stable.
content.plain: A stable behavior does not immediately lose its qualitative or quantitative character after a small perturbation.

assumptions.text: A group G acts on a set X.
An object x belongs to X.

content.caveat: Symmetry depends on the chosen object representation and transformation group.
content.exact: The symmetry group of x relative to the action of G on X is Stab_G(x) = { g in G : g·x = x }.
content.example: A square in the Euclidean plane has rotations and reflections that map the square to itself.
content.plain: Symmetry is never just “looks the same”: one must specify which transformations are allowed and what counts as unchanged.
